title: India's Extreme Poverty Falls to 2.6% as 496 Million Escape, World Bank Says
excerpt: The World Bank's October 2026 brief credits consumption growth, women's employment and food subsidies for one of the fastest poverty declines in the world — while flagging a 13-to-1 wage gap.
body:
• India's extreme poverty rate fell from 27.1% in 2011 to 2.6% in 2023, according to the World Bank's October 2026 Poverty and Equity Brief.
  • An estimated 496 million people moved above the $4.20-a-day lower-middle-income poverty line over the same period.
  • The Bank credits strong consumption growth, rising employment — especially among women — and expanded social transfers including food subsidies.
  • The gains have a limit: the top 10% of workers earn about 13 times the bottom 10%, and about 57% of India's poor live in the Uttar Pradesh-to-West Bengal belt.

India recorded one of the fastest poverty declines in the world over the past decade, with extreme poverty falling from 27.1 per cent of the population in 2011 to 2.6 per cent in 2023, the World Bank said in its October 2026 Poverty and Equity Brief. An estimated 496 million people moved out of poverty during the period.

Extreme poverty is measured against a line of $3.00 a day at 2021 purchasing power parity. On the wider lower-middle-income line of $4.20 a day, the poverty rate fell from 57.7 per cent in 2011 to 16.1 per cent in 2023, according to the brief, reported by The Hindu BusinessLine.

What drove the decline

The World Bank attributed the improvement mainly to strong consumption growth, rising employment and expanded social transfers, including food subsidies. Employment rose by about 134 million people between 2017 and 2023 — nearly twice the growth in the working-age population — with much of the increase coming from rural women entering paid work, Jagran Josh reported in its summary of the brief.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=oai2Qs6qQXQ

Non-monetary poverty fell as well. The Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative's Multidimensional Poverty Index dropped from 53.8 per cent in 2005-06 to 16.4 per cent in 2019-21, while the World Bank's own multidimensional measure stood at 15.5 per cent in 2022-23. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman attributed the trend to the government's sustained policy efforts.

"Over the past decade, India has made remarkable progress in reducing poverty across both monetary and non-monetary dimensions, recording one of the fastest poverty declines in the world."

— World Bank, India Poverty and Equity Brief, October 2026

The caveats: jobs quality and a 13-to-1 wage gap

The brief is equally clear about what has not changed. Real earnings remained broadly unchanged, and much of the new employment is in relatively low-productivity work. Median earnings among the top 10 per cent of workers were about 13 times those of the bottom 10 per cent in 2023. Youth unemployment rose from 14.6 per cent to 15.9 per cent between the first quarters of FY26 and FY27, with rural young women hit hardest.

https://x.com/TawdeVinod/status/2116134415361515888

Poverty is also geographically concentrated: about 57 per cent of India's poor live in a contiguous belt from Uttar Pradesh to West Bengal, making productive jobs in those states decisive for further progress. The Bank cautioned that its estimates rest on household consumption surveys, that some gains may reflect better measurement as well as real welfare improvements, and that surveys may understate inequality by missing consumption at the top.

What comes next

The World Bank projects a slower decline from here: the poverty rate at the $4.20-a-day line is expected to fall from 14.2 per cent in 2026 to 12.1 per cent by 2028. Those projections are indicative microsimulations and will be revised as new labour-market and survey data arrive. For the diaspora, the numbers frame both the opportunity and the limit of India's growth story — hundreds of millions of households with rising consumption, alongside a jobs-quality problem that remittances and return migration alone cannot solve.
